notes.meaning: Job states that he made a strict agreement with his eyes not to look with lust upon an unmarried woman. He knew that outward sins begin with inward thoughts and unguarded looks. By controlling his eyes, he kept his heart pure before God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the Hebrew term for virgin here refers not to a young woman, but to 'the Maiden,' an ancient title for a pagan fertility goddess.

notes.meaning: Job asks what reward an unfaithful person could expect from God on high. He knows that God brings ruin and sudden disaster on those who practice hidden evil. This healthy fear of God's righteous judgment kept him from giving in to sinful desires.

Job reminds himself that God watches every road he takes and numbers every step he makes. Nothing he did in secret could ever be hidden from the Almighty. Remembering God's all-seeing eye gave Job a strong reason to walk uprightly every day.

Job denies that he ever used lies or rushed into cheating others in his business dealings. He asks God to place his life on honest scales to test him. He is confident that any fair trial will prove his true integrity and honesty.

Job invites a curse on himself if his feet wandered from God's way, if his heart coveted what his eyes saw, or if stolen goods stained his hands. In that case, he says another person should eat what he planted, and his crops should be pulled up by the roots. He is willing to suffer severe loss if he acquired anything unjustly.

Job declares that he never lusted after his neighbor's wife or waited by her door for a secret meeting. If he had committed such a betrayal, he accepts that his own wife might be made a slave to grind grain or be taken by other men. He recognized that breaking another man's home deserved a dreadful penalty.

Job explains that adultery is a shameful crime that human judges ought to punish. Beyond that, lust acts like a raging fire that burns down to the place of destruction and ruins all of a person's life and wealth. Such sins provoke God's holy anger and destroy domestic peace.

Job gave his male and female servants a fair hearing whenever they had a grievance against him. He remembered that God is the Master of all and would soon call him to give an account. Since the same Creator formed both master and servant in the womb, Job treated his workers as fellow human beings with equal dignity.

Job defended himself against the accusation that he neglected the poor and made widows weep from waiting for help. He did not hoard his food for himself, but shared his meals with orphans at his own table. From his earliest youth, he cared for the fatherless like a parent and guided the widow with loving counsel.

Job never ignored a needy person who was shivering without clothes. Instead, he sheared his own sheep to make warm garments for the destitute. Those he clothed were so relieved that their whole bodies blessed Job for his generous care.

Job never used his power or his influence in the city court to bully a helpless orphan. If he had ever lifted his fist against the weak because judges were on his side, he calls down a curse for his own arm to be torn from its socket. He believed an arm used to crush the poor deserved to be broken.

Job explains what kept him from oppressing anyone: he lived in holy awe of God's majesty and judgment. He knew he could never stand before God's power or escape His righteous punishment if he harmed the poor. A deep reverence for God is the best guard against abusing others.

Job insists that he never placed his hope or security in piles of gold. He had great wealth, but he did not take pride in his own success or let possessions become his chief joy. He treated money as a tool to do good rather than an idol to worship.

Job never took part in the ancient worship of the sun and moon. He was not tempted to blow a kiss with his hand to praise the heavenly lights as gods. To do so would have been an open crime that denied the true God who created them all.

Job did not celebrate when disaster struck his enemies, nor did he gloat over their downfall. He kept a close guard over his words, refusing to curse his foes or wish for their death. True godliness teaches love and restraint even toward those who hate us.

Job's servants could testify that no visitor ever left his estate without plenty of meat to eat. He never left a traveler stranded outside in the cold street at night. His front doors were always open to welcome strangers with generous hospitality.

Job states that he did not hide his wrongdoing in secret like Adam did in the garden, trying to cover his guilt. Nor was he a coward who stayed inside and kept quiet out of fear of what powerful families or crowds might say. Whenever he made a mistake, he was ready to confess it openly and do what was right.

differ.view: Methodist commentators understand the phrase as a direct reference to the first man, Adam, hiding his transgression in Paradise.
While early translations rendered the words simply as 'after the manner of men,' later Lutheran scholars maintain that the verse specifically points to the historical fall of Adam in Eden.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that the Hebrew word can point to Adam shifting blame to Eve, but it can also be translated more generally as 'like men.'

notes.meaning: Job longs for a fair hearing and puts his signature to his defense. He calls on the Almighty to answer him and challenges his accusers to write down their formal charges on a scroll. He is so certain of his innocence that he welcomes a full legal examination.

Job says he would wear his opponent's written charges on his shoulder like a badge of honor and place them on his head like a royal crown. He would gladly explain every single step of his life to God. He feels confident enough to approach the Judge not as a cowering criminal, but with the bold dignity of a prince.

Job ends his speech by declaring that his fields never cried out against him for stolen land or unpaid workers. If he took crops without paying or drove landowners to despair, he asks that thorns and foul weeds grow instead of wheat and barley. With these final words of defense, Job finishes his long debate with his friends.
